title: Dasam Granth Explained for IB World Religions
summary: Dasam Granth explained for IB World Religions SL, including its origins, contents, authorship debate, Sikh interpretations, themes, and key concepts.
body_markdown:
The **Dasam Granth** is a collection of devotional, philosophical, heroic, and narrative compositions associated with Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru. It stands separately from the Guru Granth Sahib and does not hold the same status as the eternal Guru. Yet particular compositions remain important in Sikh prayer, initiation, theology, and collective memory.


For IB World Religions SL, focus on three questions: what does the collection contain, why are its authorship and authority debated, and how do particular passages influence lived Sikh practice? Religious texts do not exist only as words. Their significance also depends on how communities recite, interpret, contest, and embody them.


### The Dasam Granth at a glance


Use this checklist as your foundation:


- **Name:** *Dasam Granth* , commonly understood as the collection associated with the tenth Guru
- **Original-language title:** ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ in Gurmukhi
- **Association:** Guru Gobind Singh, 1666-1708
- **Compilation:** The present collection was assembled after his lifetime from compositions and manuscripts associated with him and his court
- **Languages:** Primarily Braj, with Punjabi, Persian, and other linguistic forms represented
- **Themes:** Divine transcendence, justice, courage, moral struggle, political integrity, and resistance to oppression
- **Status:** Influential and respected, but distinct from the Guru Granth Sahib
- **Central debate:** Whether all, some, or most compositions were written directly by Guru Gobind Singh


RevisionDojo's[notes on the collation of the Adi Granth and Dasam Granth](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-732-collation-and-development-adi-granth-dasam-gra-93267/notes) provide a syllabus-focused introduction to these distinctions.


### What does Dasam Granth mean?


*Dasam* means “tenth,” while *granth* means a bound text, book, or compilation. The title associates the collection with the tenth Guru, but it does not settle who wrote every line. A title can express inherited authority without functioning as a modern declaration of single authorship.


The collection is also called the *Dasven Patshah ka Granth* , meaning the granth of the tenth sovereign or Guru. Guru Gobind Singh is remembered as a spiritual teacher and as the founder of the Khalsa, the initiated Sikh community established in 1699. The collection's combination of devotion, discipline, and heroic imagery becomes clearer within that setting.


### Dasam Granth and Guru Granth Sahib are not equivalent


The most important correction for an IB answer is simple: the Dasam Granth is not the Guru Granth Sahib.


The **Guru Granth Sahib** is recognized as the eternal Guru of the Sikhs. It contains hymns associated with Sikh Gurus and selected *bhagats* , or devotional poet-saints from different backgrounds. It receives distinctive ceremonial authority in the *gurdwara* .


The Dasam Granth remains a separate collection. It may be studied, quoted, and recited, but it is not universally enthroned as the eternal Guru alongside the Guru Granth Sahib. RevisionDojo's[guide to the Guru Granth Sahib](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-731-the-guru-granth-sahib-revelation-and-composition/notes) explains why Sikhs honour the revealed Word rather than worshipping a physical object.


A strong response should therefore avoid calling both works simply “the Sikh holy book.” That phrase conceals differences in status, function, and community reception.

### What is inside the collection?


The Dasam Granth is better understood as an anthology than as one continuous argument. Its compositions differ in language, genre, subject, and tone.


### Jaap Sahib and Akal Ustat


**Jaap Sahib** praises the attributes of the divine. Its many names and descriptions emphasize that ultimate reality exceeds any single label, form, nation, or religious identity. It supports the Sikh concept of **Akal Purakh** , the Timeless Being.


**Akal Ustat** , or “Praise of the Timeless One,” similarly celebrates divine universality. Passages associated with it are often discussed in relation to human equality and the limitations of narrow social divisions. Students exploring language can consult RevisionDojo's notes on[Gurbani, Gurmukhi, and scriptural interpretation](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-733-interpretation-and-language-gurbani-gurmukhi-a-93268/notes) .


### Bachittar Natak and heroic compositions


**Bachittar Natak** , meaning “Wondrous Drama,” presents material concerning Guru Gobind Singh's lineage, mission, and historical circumstances. It should not be treated as a modern autobiography. Its purpose is theological as well as narrative, placing human action within **hukam** , the divine order or command.


Works including **Chandi Charitar** , **Chandi di Var** , and sections of **Chaubis Avtar** adapt older South Asian narratives. One interpretation reads their battles symbolically as struggles against ego, injustice, and moral weakness. Another emphasizes martial formation, arguing that heroic language cultivated the courage needed to resist persecution and defend others.


### Zafarnama and disputed narratives


The **Zafarnama** , or “Epistle of Victory,” is a Persian letter traditionally understood as Guru Gobind Singh's address to the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. It condemns broken promises and presents truthfulness as superior to political power. Victory is moral before it is military.


The **Hikayats** , meaning “tales,” explore conduct, deception, judgment, and power. Other sections, especially **Charitropakhyan** , remain disputed because of their complex depictions of sexuality, manipulation, and human behaviour.


### Why is authorship debated?


The debate should be described rather than “solved” in an IB essay. Many Sikhs accept the collection as the work of Guru Gobind Singh, sometimes allowing that scribes or court poets helped record and arrange it. Differences in style can be explained through the Guru's command of several languages and literary genres. From this perspective, devotion, heroic narrative, and warnings about moral danger serve a coherent educational purpose.


Other Sikh interpreters and academic scholars argue for composite authorship. They attribute certain works to Guru Gobind Singh while questioning whether every composition came from him. Their arguments consider manuscript history, vocabulary, literary form, and variations among early collections.


Questioning complete authorship does not automatically mean rejecting Guru Gobind Singh or Sikh tradition. Likewise, traditional attribution should not be dismissed as intellectually simplistic. A practical third position concentrates on compositions established within Sikh worship without attempting to resolve the origin of every section.


### Interpretations across Sikh communities


Within mainstream Khalsa practice associated with the **Sikh Rehat Maryada** , compositions including Jaap Sahib, the Ten Sawayyas, and Benti Chaupai appear in daily prayer or initiation contexts. Their use gives parts of the Dasam tradition an enduring ritual role.


**Nihang Sikhs** , known for preserving a strongly martial Khalsa identity, generally grant the collection extensive authority and feature its heroic language prominently in religious life. Some Nihang settings give it a ceremonial position that is not typical of every gurdwara.


Other Sikhs may accept particular compositions while disputing the authorship or authority of the complete anthology. The picture is not a simple choice between acceptance and rejection. Authority can be liturgical, devotional, historical, or canonical, and those categories need not overlap.


### Connecting the text to IB questions


The[three fundamental questions in IB World Religions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-116-the-three-fundamental-questions-and-the-world-93046/notes) turn textual knowledge into analysis.


### What is the human condition?


Humans can pursue devotion and justice, but they remain vulnerable to **haumai** , ego-centredness, fear, deception, and attachment. Praise poetry directs attention beyond the self, while narrative passages dramatize the consequences of misused power.


### Where are we going?


Sikh thought points toward **mukti** , liberation from ego and rebirth through alignment with the divine. Devotional compositions emphasize God's timeless reality, while heroic passages suggest that spiritual orientation should change how people confront injustice. RevisionDojo's explanation of[jot, mukti, hukam, and the five khands](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-743-eschatology-jot-mukti-hukam-and-the-five-khands/notes) develops these concepts.


### How do we get there?


The collection points toward remembrance of God, disciplined prayer, truthful conduct, courage, and resistance to tyranny. These belong within wider Sikh teachings such as **nam japna** , remembering the divine Name; **kirat karni** , earning honestly; and **vand chhakna** , sharing with others.


### Connecting the Dasam Granth to the five themes


IB theme Dasam Granth connection


Rituals Jaap Sahib, Sawayyas, and Benti Chaupai contribute to prayer and Khalsa initiation.


Sacred texts Its compilation and authorship show how communities establish textual boundaries.


Doctrines and beliefs Devotional works explore Akal Purakh, hukam, transcendence, and equality.


Religious experience Recitation can encourage disciplined attention, courage, and humility.


Ethics and moral conduct The Zafarnama raises questions about truth, promises, leadership, and oppression.


Do not merely name a theme. Explain the connection through a specific composition and interpretation. RevisionDojo's[complete Sikhism revision notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-7-sikhism/notes) can place each example within the wider course.


### How to use the Dasam Granth in an IB response


Begin with a precise claim: “The authority of the Dasam Granth is layered because particular compositions have established liturgical roles even though authorship of the complete collection remains debated.”


Then identify a composition, explain its teaching or function, connect it to an IB question and theme, and introduce a contrasting interpretation. Avoid making one Sikh group speak for all Sikhs. Finish by explaining why the difference matters.

Use the[IB World Religions Study Notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions) for context and[Sikhism Flashcards](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-7-sikhism/flashcards) for terminology. The Questionbank, AI Chat, and Grading tools help test whether an explanation moves beyond description. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams build timed confidence, while the Coursework Library and Tutors support deeper questions about textual authority.


### A text becomes clearer when its roles are separated


The Dasam Granth becomes confusing when every question is forced into one category. Authorship is not identical to canonical status. Canonical status is not identical to ritual use. Ritual use is not identical across Sikh communities.


Once those distinctions are clear, the collection becomes a valuable case study in how sacred literature can praise the divine, form ethical character, inspire resistance to injustice, and generate internal debate. The strongest student asks not only whether a text matters, but to whom, in what way, through which composition, and with what consequences. RevisionDojo provides the knowledge, practice, feedback, and human support needed to turn those questions into a precise and respectful argument.
